• 14 November 2026 · Dispatch
    London Pride @home
    Pinter and Fuller’s have put London Pride in a kit you brew on the kitchen counter, with a different yeast in the sachet. What has to stay the same for it still to be Pride?
    Read the dispatch →

• 14 November 2026 · Essay
    Pride Unfiltered. The biggest launch in a generation?
    In February 2017 Fuller’s called London Pride Unfiltered its biggest beer launch in a generation. It was the official beer partner of the Pride in London parade the next summer. The brewery has never said when it stopped making it.
    Read the essay →

• 9 November 2026 · Essay
    A Cider of His Own
    Jeffrey House spent ten years selling other people’s cider in America, losing Fuller’s to Grolsch and Blackthorn to Miller. So he made one of his own, sold 1,200 cases of it to a supermarket before he had bottled a drop, and built ACE into a brand he would be hired back to rescue.
    Read the essay →

• 6 November 2026 · Essay
    The First Friday of Christmas
    Tuborg’s Julebryg goes on sale at 20:59 Danish time on the first Friday of November, and not a minute before. A Norwegian king once made Christmas brewing compulsory, and in 1975 Fritz Maytag brewed one in San Francisco that, as far as he could discover, was the only real one in the world.
    Read the essay →

• 6 November 2026 · Essay
    Winter is not Christmas
    A winter beer and a Christmas beer are different things. In 1971 Young’s renamed an old Burton ale Winter Warmer, four years before Fritz Maytag walked round the brewery looking for something else.
    Read the essay →

• 2 November 2026 · Essay
    Voice of the Fire
    Harvey’s have brewed in Lewes since about 1820 and beside the Ouse since 1838. They make Bonfire Boy for the fifth of November and ferment it with a yeast that came down from York by train in 1957.
    Read the essay →

• 2 November 2026 · Note
    Roast is not smoke
    Harvey’s use black malt to give Bonfire Boy its suggestion of smoke. Black malt comes from an 1817 drum, borrowed from coffee roasting, which gave brewers their colour with the fire kept off the grain.
    Read the note →

• 26 October 2026 · Essay
    Season of the Witch
    The Green Man carvings are medieval, the pub name is centuries old, and the pagan reading only dates from 1939. On folk horror, Rentaghost, pumpkin ale, green hop beer and cider at Halloween.
    Read the essay →

• 24 October 2026 · Essay
    The Unholy Trinity
    Three of the autumn’s great nights fall inside a single week. Halloween on the thirty-first, Lewes Bonfire on the fifth, and J-dag, when Tuborg's Christmas beer goes on sale at 20:59 on the first Friday of November. One essay each.
    Read the essay →

• 20 October 2026 · Essay
    Before he could sell ESB to America, he had to sell it to Fuller’s
    Jeffrey House remembers the first pour at the College Inn in Seattle on 3 November 1987. He had been trying to get it there for years. When it arrived, American brewers found more in it than a good pint.
    Read the essay →

• 17 October 2026 · Note
    Why Firestone Walker chose Fuller’s yeast
    The American influence on British beer is usually told through hops. This one runs the other way. Firestone Walker ran beer trials, the Wyeast strain Walker remembers as a Fuller’s ESB yeast beat Chico even though Chico was cleaner, and taming its flocculation took them a few years. What replaced it is still, in co-founder David Walker’s words, essentially a Fullers/London yeast.
    Read the note →

• 23 September 2026 · Note
    Tegernseer on Draught, and Where
    Tegernseer Hell is one of Bavaria’s most sought-after lagers and reaches British bars in small, unpublicised quantities. Cross-referencing our own live tap data finds eleven UK venues that have poured it.
    Read the note →

• 20 September 2026 · Essay
    Everything Traditional About Oktoberfest Is Younger Than the Tent
    In 1898 five strawmen for the Münchner Kindl brewery bid for five Oktoberfest stalls. They went to Nuremberg publican Georg Lang, who joined them into a hall for 6,000. The other restaurateurs sued the city and lost.
    Read the essay →

• 19 September 2026 · Guide
    UK Oktoberfest Events 2026
    Munich’s new mayor needed two blows of the hammer at noon today. If that gave you ideas: seventy-six British Oktoberfests, twelve of which pour at least one of Munich's six Wiesn beers, and one “all six” claim that names five.
    Read the guide →

• 18 September 2026 · Essay
    September is Oktoberfest
    The 191st Wiesn opens tomorrow at noon, and the beer in the tents is not the beer the festival started with. Munich changed it, America kept the old one, Britain borrowed the words, and twelve of the sixteen days fall in September.
    Read the essay →

• 17 September 2026 · Essay
    Cask Ale Week: the Cellar, the Plaque and Thirteen Pints
    Cask Ale Week runs 17–27 September, with more than 10,000 pubs signed up. What cask actually is, what the plaque on the door promises, thirteen pints worth chasing this week, and the numbers behind a revival led by drinkers in their twenties.
    Read the essay →

• 3 September 2026 · Essay
    The Geography of Sobriety
    How the move of Fleet Street’s papers to Wapping in 1986 and the growth of Canary Wharf from 1988 changed where London’s journalists and City workers drank.
    Read the essay →

• 2 September 2026 · Essay
    Old Haunts of the Square Mile
    Balls Brothers, Corney & Barrow, Davy's, All Bar One and Pitcher & Piano: five City bar chains of the 1990s, and what became of their sites.
    Read the essay →

• 30 August 2026 · Essay
    Ghosts of Baddow Brewery
    Baddow Brewery stopped brewing in 1927. Nearly a century later, 30 of the 61 pubs associated with it are still serving drinkers, from Great Baddow itself out to the Essex coast. Fourteen have been replaced or converted, fifteen have gone, two remain honestly unknown. A stone's throw from the old brewing ground, Chelmsford Brewing Company has brewed at Brewery Fields since 2017.
    Read the essay →

• 17 August 2026 · Essay
    Revivals, recreations or just echoes?
    British beer is having a revival revival. Old names are back on the bar: some painstakingly reconstructed, some entirely new beers wearing dead men's clothes. Divers and KU Leuven are trying to recover the yeast DNA from an 1864 Guinness shipwreck bottle. A field guide to what's actually being resurrected: recipe, yeast, water, brewery, people, badge, or nothing but the name.
    Read the essay →

• 5 August 2026 · Essay
    Davy's: a century and a half of sawdust and candles
    Founded off the Strand in 1870, Davy's still lists fifteen London sites of its own, fourteen of them trading, plus three El Vino sisters brought in in 2015. In 2007 the chain had 37 sites; more than half of the family-name ones have gone since. Bangers, Bangers Too, the Crusting Pipe (closed just before Christmas 2025 after a 45-year run), the City Boot twice, City FOB, Skinkers, and two different lives of the Tappit Hen. The story of a chain slowly editing itself down.
    Read the essay →

• 31 July 2026 · Essay
    Celebrity-Owned Pubs Worth the Pint (Not Just the Autograph)
    News this week that James Blunt has bought a second London pub, The Carpenter's Arms in Hammersmith, is a decent excuse to ask the only useful question about celebrity-owned pubs: which are actually worth the pint? Verdicts and PINtPOINT deep links for Ian McKellen's Dickens-listed Thames boozer, Blunt's Chelsea local, Guy Ritchie's Fitzrovia gastropub, Jeremy Clarkson's Cotswolds farm-pub, and seven more.
    Read the essay →

• 29 July 2026 · Essay
    The Green Triangle and the Oldest Trademark in British Beer
    On 1 January 1876 Britain's first registered trade mark went to a beer: Bass Brewery's red triangle, UK Trade Mark No. 1. A hundred and fifty years later, to the year, PINtPOINT needed a shape to single out the best pub around. What else could we pick? Why the geometry, why green not red, and why on a small screen at the end of a long day the fastest way to say 'this one' is still a triangle.
    Read the essay →

• 17 July 2026 · Essay
    The Anti-Check-In: Why We Skip the Feed
    Untappd is a social network first and a beer database second. Its tap lists only get fresh when someone posts publicly about a pint. PINtPOINT lets you improve any tap list with one tap and no check-in, because contributing to shared data shouldn't demand personal consumption or a social broadcast. Why fresh tap lists shouldn't depend on social posting.
    Read the note →

• 15 July 2026 · Essay
    It's Not Just the Sunshine: Your Holiday Beer Really Is a Different Beer
    The Estrella you drank in Barcelona is 5.4%; the one they pour in Manchester is 4.6%, brewed by Damm at the Bedford Eagle Brewery it bought in 2022. Madri Excepcional is brewed at Tadcaster in Yorkshire. What CAMRA's July 2026 Beer in the UK Report says, and why the app cares.
    Read the explainer →

• 14 July 2026 · Essay
    The Beer Final We Almost Had: England vs Spain
    Argentina beat England 2-1 in the semi-final on Wednesday. This piece was drafted for the beer final we might have had: a Berlin rematch of English cask against Spain's Iberian craft column. Publishing it anyway as the parallel-timeline read. Draught Bass hat-trick, a 101st-minute ghost goal, Estrella Damm and La Pirata Black Block. The Pub VAR booth stands by its verdict. The actual final (Argentina vs Spain) follows.
    Read the parallel-timeline verdict →

• 3 July 2026 · Note
    Norman Balon: London's Last Great Rude Landlord
    The Coach and Horses landlord who ran the Greek Street pub for sixty-three years and made a public brand of his own rudeness has died aged 99. On the fortnightly Private Eye lunch, the Waterhouse play, the 2005 licensing regulations he wouldn't sit down and read, and why a room isn't the same room once the person who kept it wrong on purpose has gone.
    Read the note →

• 30 June 2026 · Note
    Humphrey Smith: British Beer's Great Awkward Character
    The Samuel Smith's beer baron who ran Britain's strangest pub chain by his own private rule has died aged 81. On cheap pints, dark wood, shire horses, boarded-up villages and a row over an air freshener, and on why the whole thing may become easier without him and also less peculiar.
    Read the note →

• 27 June 2026 · Guide
    Loaded’s World Cup Canon: From Crisps to Vodka
    The canonical record of Loaded magazine’s recurring World Cup format. The first five editions ran in fifteen months from September 1994 to December 1995, Crisp, Washing Powder, Lager’lympics, Cereals and Vodka, and define the format at its peak.
    Read the guide →

• 25 June 2026 · Guide
    Lager’lympics: Loaded Magazine’s Lost 1995 Lager World Cup, Found
    The full record of the Lager’lympics, Loaded magazine’s 1995 Lager World Cup, published in the ‘What’s For Tea Love?’ supplement. 62 lagers, a knockout bracket and drunk-panel scoring. Budvar beat Molson 178 to 98 in the final.
    Read the guide →

• 23 June 2026 · Essay
    Before Kick-Off: Why English Cask Has the Advantage
    The football is heading to the business end. The Beer World Cup is heading the same way. With the Perfect Pint Promise just launched and heritage cask back on the rise, the case for English cask is loud and current. Greene King has sold Old Speckled Hen to Spanish lager giant Damm, Draught Bass is back on more than a thousand hand pumps, and JW Lees has relaunched cask Boddingtons. The squad of eleven hand-pulled pints we'd send into a Beer World Cup, and why cask is the one format the world can't quite copy.
    Read the essay →

• 19 June 2026 · Guide
    World Cup 2026 Stadium Beer Map: Help Us Find Good Beer Near The Grounds
    The World Cup is here, across 16 host stadiums in North America. We mapped the bars, pubs, breweries, taprooms, bottle shops and beer gardens that can actually help fans before or after a match. A first pass, not the final whistle. Some host areas came together cleanly. Some are awkward. Open PINtPOINT near a host stadium and add what we missed.
    Read the guide →

• 19 June 2026 · Essay
    Beer World Cup XI: 48 Nations, Real Fixtures, Stupidly Serious Beer Results
    The football teams play on the pitch. The beers play in the pub. Every country in the World Cup gets a beer squad; the actual draw drives the matchups, and Pub VAR may upset the scores. A serialised editorial tournament loosely based on a distant memory of Loaded magazine's lost Beer World Cup.
    Read the essay →

• 2 June 2026 · Essay
    Beerology: The Anatomy of a Pint
    What does this beer actually feel like to drink? Eight axes (Body, Bitterness, Sweetness, Roast, Fruit, Finish, Softness, Complexity) plus four drinker cues, a drinkability bucket, and one plain-English gut-take sentence per beer. Built for the 800-millisecond tap-list decision; honest about the sour and Belgian-yeast styles it doesn't cover. The capstone of the four-essay arc on choosing the right pint.
    Read the essay →

• 31 May 2026 · Essay
    Following the Firkin trail(s)…
    In 1979 David Bruce opened the Goose & Firkin in Elephant and Castle. By 1995 the chain had 44 pubs, 19 of them brewing on site. On 8 October 1999 the brewing stopped, and that, not the 2001 brand-discontinuation, is when Firkin actually died. The 12 original London Firkin sites, plotted on a 1990 paper leaflet, deliberately traced the outline of a dog's head. Companion: walk the route in PINtPOINT's new Hall-of-Fame crawl.
    Read the essay →

• 24 May 2026 · Essay
    Anchor Brewing's British heritage runs deeper than people realise
    Two of Anchor's signature beers came home from an October 1975 English brewery tour. Liberty Ale, the one everyone credits to it, predates the trip by six months on David Burkhart's dating. The Great American Beer Festival was modelled on CAMRA's GBBF. Anchor first reached British draught in November 1991, in borrowed Fuller's kegs, and a West Yorkshire distributor kept it there for fifteen years after. The companion to Friday's revival piece: the case that Anchor's identity was always partly English, and what that means for a return to UK taps.
    Read the essay →

• 22 May 2026 · Essay
    Anchor Brewing looks to be coming back. Nobody will say when.
    Construction crews at Potrero Hill, an owner who has said almost nothing in public, and a 2027 date nobody official has given. Updated in November with the label approvals and the business-name filing.
    Read the essay →

• 20 May 2026 · Essay
    Under the Hood: How PINtDEXTER Picks Your Pint
    The engineering follow-up to the recommender essay. The four layers PINtDEXTER stacks under the hood (preference capture, manual sliders, per-beer LLM-inferred flavour DNA, and venue-aware scoring), and the misclassified pale lager that exposed the most recent fix. For the data-science curious.
    Read the essay →

• 16 May 2026 · Note
    Save Our Pubs, In One Pub: The Bell at Ingatestone
    We walked into the Bell to claim a free pint of Telegraph Ale on Saturday. PINtPOINT's Financial Pressure Index also flags the same building as Struggling: rateable value up 74% since 2023, FPI 44.38/100. The campaign's structural argument, made personal, on the bar in front of us.
    Read the note →

• 16 May 2026 · Note
    Almost Two Pubs a Day Are Closing. The Telegraph's Answer Is a Free Pint.
    Saturday 16 May is the Telegraph's National Pub Day. Renegade Brewery, the West Berkshire outfit that took on the West Berkshire estate after the 2023 collapse, has brewed Telegraph Ale, a 4% cask English bitter, for over 250 participating pubs nationwide. The campaign sits inside Save Our Pubs, the Telegraph's response to a closure rate the paper put at four pubs a day.
    Read the note →

• 14 May 2026 · Essay
    From Half of British Beer to Half a Percent: What Happened to Mild
    In 1959 mild was still half the beer Britain drank. By 2011 it was 0.5%. How Britain's everyday beer became a rarity, and why Mild May is trying to bring it back. Pattinson, Cornell and Boak & Bailey on the collapse; the modern fork between stalwarts and craft revisionists.
    Read the essay →

• 8 May 2026 · Note
    The Sparkler Question: A Field Guide to Britain's Quietest Cask Argument
    A small nozzle. A 140-year argument. Mostly a Northern tradition, with London outposts at the Queen's Arms and the Punch Tavern. From 14 May the Whippet adds a sparklered Boddingtons to the Liverpool Street commute.
    Read the note →

• 5 May 2026 · Note
    The Whippet at Liverpool Street
    The Whippet still is not pouring Augustiner, but it has quietly built one of the more unusual lager line-ups near Liverpool Street: Bitburger, Kutna Hora, Tegernseer and Benediktiner, alongside Boddingtons cask through a sparkler. Only the Tegernseer is brewed in Bavaria.
    Read the note →

• 1 May 2026 · Note
    Radio City Turns 7: 7 Cans, 7 Sins, 35 Launch Venues, and One Big Saturday in Chelmsford
    On Saturday 9 May 2026, Radio City Beer Works in Radley Green throws its biggest birthday yet, preceded two days earlier by the nationwide can launch of the Seven Deadly Sins. Lust × Black Iris (Strawberry Vanilla Pastry Sour), Wrath × Ampersand (Southern Hemisphere IPA), Gluttony × Vibrant Forest (Imperial Stout 8.4%), and four more. Full launch-venue locator inside.
    Read the note →

• 1 May 2026 · Note
    Blackhorse Beer Mile 4th Birthday: All 10 Participating Venues with PINtPOINT Links
    On Sunday 3 May 2026, Walthamstow's brewery-district mile turns four with an all-day, free-entry, family-friendly takeover across 10 east-London craft venues: Big Penny Social, Exale, Signature, Borough Wines, Burnt Faith, East London Brewing Co, plus 40FT, Hackney Church, Renegade and Pretty Decent. Every venue with a PINtPOINT deeplink plus the canonical Hall of Fame crawl.
    Read the note →

• 30 April 2026 · Note
    Augustiner on Draft, Finally: Six Confirmed UK Pubs Pouring It
    Augustiner Helles landed on UK draught in November 2025 via James Clay & Sons with no public venue list. PINtPOINT cross-references public Untappd data to confirm six: King's Arms in Bethnal Green, Café Beermoth and Society in Manchester, Bavaria Brauhaus in Glasgow, Blind Jack's in Knaresborough and the Oil Basin Brewhouse in Worcester. No news on the Whippet, but we are still hopeful.
    Read the note →

• 29 April 2026 · Note
    12 Years of Bosko: All 12 UK Venues Pouring Pressure Drop's West Coast IPA on 1 May
    Twelve years ago Pressure Drop released their first batch of Bosko, a 6.5% West Coast IPA brewed in a Hackney railway arch. Friday 1 May 2026, twelve UK venues are simultaneously putting it on the lines. Every launch venue with PINtPOINT links, plus the back-story on the beer.
    Read the note →

• 27 April 2026 · Essay
    Left Field Beer and the Price of American Craft in Britain
    Fresh American imports (Trillium, Hop Butcher) alongside European specialists like Arpus and CoolHead and championed UK indies including DEYA and Buxton, all curated from a single Solihull shop. With the deep-dive on why drinking American craft properly is so expensive over here.
    Read the essay →

• 24 April 2026 · Essay
    Bass Pale Ale: The Red Triangle That Took an English Beer Global
    The red triangle was the first trade mark registered in the United Kingdom, and it travelled to India, Russia and America on hard Burton water, coke-malted pale grain and clear glass. From a Burton brewery in 1777 through the Bass Charrington years and the Molson Coors split, to the 1,000 pubs now pouring Draught Bass.
    Read the essay →

• 20 April 2026 · Postcard
    A Postcard from London: From Porter and IPA to the Kernel
    The third in the trilogy. London is one of the oldest beer cities in the world, but the version you can drink now dates from 2009: a comeback layered over an inheritance. Porter, IPA, Ind Coope and Charrington, then the long gap, then The Kernel on Druid Street and a new scene built on top of the ruins.
    Read the postcard →

• 19 April 2026 · Guide
    Walking the Ted Lasso Pub Trail in Richmond: From Crown & Anchor to Richmond Hill
    The Crown & Anchor exterior is The Prince's Head on Richmond Green. One stop is a Richmond Hill finisher with the kind of Thames-bend view the show keeps coming back to. A four-stop walking pub trail for fans of the show, and a shortlist of the wider Richmond craft-beer scene worth a pint while you're there.
    Read the guide →

• 16 April 2026 · Postcard
    A Postcard from Melbourne: The City That Built a Craft-Beer Scene on Bars, Not Breweries
    Companion to the San Diego piece, and its structural opposite. San Diego built a craft-beer capital brewery-first; Melbourne did it bar-first. Catfish, Local Taphouse, Cookie, Hippo, Boilermaker: a scene that turned curation into a category of its own.
    Read the postcard →

• 12 April 2026 · Essay · Reference
    The Drinker's Guide to Hops: What Each Variety Actually Tastes Like
    A drinker-first reference to the 30-odd hops you're most likely to meet on a UK or European bar (Cascade, Citra, Mosaic, EKG, Saaz and the rest), organised by a six-category flavour framework that collapses Drexler's unwieldy 107 descriptors into something you can actually hold in your head.
    Read the guide →

• 9 April 2026 · Postcard
    A Postcard from San Diego: Where the West Coast IPA Grew Up
    Karl Strauss in 1989. Stone and Ballast Point in 1996. A hop arms race through the 2000s that perfected the West Coast IPA. A tour of how San Diego quietly became the IPA capital, and where in North Park, Miramar, and La Jolla to drink its legacy today.
    Read the postcard →

• 5 April 2026 · Guide
    The Chelmsford Beer Mile: A Live Guide to the Route
    When we wrote this, eight specialist venues sat within a mile of each other (bottle shops, a brewpub, railway arch taprooms). This guide walks them in the right order, with live tap lists for every stop, plus a footnote on Baddow Brewery (1798–1927) and the forty-year gap before Chelmsford Brewing Company started up in 2017.
    Read the guide →

• 29 March 2026 · Essay
    What's Wrong With Beer Recommendation Systems (And What PINtPOINT Does Differently)
    A response to Ethan Haley's Untappd-as-a-recommender analysis and NYC Data Science's Ninkasi project. Three walls rating-based recommenders hit (cold start, popularity bias, geography-blindness) and how PINtDEXTER layers Sip-or-Skip, Head-to-Head and venue-aware scoring to answer the different question a drinker is actually asking.
    Read the essay →
